szoveg_eredeti:
Artificial Intelligence Enhances Surgical Pathology Diagnosis, Biomarker Prediction, and Operative Decision Support

Advances in computational pathology and deep learning are actively redefining the interface between surgical oncologists and pathologists by converting routine digitized tissue slides into rich diagnostic, prognostic, and predictive datasets. According to a comprehensive scientific review published in Surgical and Experimental Pathology by researchers Umang K. Agrawal, Sakshi Jaiswal, and Deepanshu Singh, artificial intelligence algorithms are demonstrating diagnostic accuracy comparable to expert pathologists across diverse malignancies, including breast, prostate, colorectal, lung, and gastrointestinal cancers. The transition from conventional microscopy of physical glass slides to digital whole-slide imaging systems has fundamentally changed modern diagnostic pathways. Rather than serving merely as static electronic records, high-resolution digitized slides allow complex computational models to evaluate microscopic architecture, cellular density, and spatial relationships that often escape conventional manual visual examination under a standard light microscope.

Histopathological evaluation has long functioned as the indispensable cornerstone of clinical cancer management, establishing definitive diagnoses, grading cellular differentiation, guiding resection margins, and directing both systemic and surgical therapeutic strategies. Traditional workflows have historically depended on pathologists manually scanning glass slides to identify atypical tissue structures, count mitotic events, and estimate margin clearances. However, modern oncological care increasingly demands individualized precision, placing substantial strain on pathology laboratories confronted with escalating caseloads, diagnostic complexity, and documented observer variability. To address these workflow constraints, computational pathology leverages machine learning models that extract quantitative patterns from tissue specimens. While traditional machine learning frameworks required labor-intensive manual feature engineering to isolate variables like nuclear pleomorphism and glandular morphology, modern deep learning architectures bypass manual feature extraction entirely, learning complex diagnostic representations directly from raw digital image pixels.

The rapid acceleration of computational pathology stems from the synergistic convergence of gigapixel whole-slide imaging technology and deep convolutional neural networks. Modern whole-slide scanners digitize conventional glass slides at extremely high resolutions, preserving sub-cellular details comparable to high-magnification optical microscopes while generating analysable electronic files. Convolutional neural networks analyze these massive image datasets using layered hierarchical computational structures. Early network layers typically detect elementary morphological features, including tissue borders, cellular edges, and simple textures, whereas deeper neural layers progressively synthesize these basic inputs into complex pathological structures, capturing glandular architecture, nuclear atypia, and stromal interactions. Multi-institutional clinical validations, such as landmark investigations by Campanella and colleagues, have shown that deep learning models can achieve near-expert diagnostic sensitivity in identifying prostate carcinoma, basal cell carcinoma, and metastatic breast cancer cells within complex whole-slide preparations.

Tumour grading represents another critical domain where artificial intelligence provides substantial clinical standardization by mitigating subjective human variability. Histological grading systems assess cellular differentiation, mitotic activity, and structural disruption to determine biological aggressiveness, yet intermediate-grade lesions frequently exhibit substantial interobserver disagreement among reviewing pathologists. In breast cancer, deep learning models automated the scoring of tubule formation, nuclear pleomorphism, and mitotic figures defined by the Nottingham Histologic Score, achieving objective quantification across whole tissue sections. Similarly, in prostate oncology, where Gleason grading dictates whether a patient undergoes radical prostatectomy or active surveillance, convolutional algorithms evaluated glandular patterns across entire biopsy cores, matching the grading fidelity of experienced uropathologists. In colorectal carcinoma and soft tissue sarcomas, computational systems differentiate complex histological subtypes, objectively measure tumour budding, quantify invasive margins, and profile tumour heterogeneity across broad tissue sections.

Beyond standard histological categorization, one of the most clinically transformative capabilities of artificial intelligence is predicting underlying genetic alterations directly from routine haematoxylin and eosin-stained slides. Contemporary precision oncology heavily depends on expensive, specialized ancillary testing such as immunohistochemistry, fluorescence in situ hybridization, and next-generation sequencing to detect actionable oncogenic targets. Deep learning models reveal that genetic and epigenetic mutations impart subtle, reproducible morphological alterations in cellular architecture, nuclear chromatin distribution, and stromal organization. Researchers demonstrated that computational platforms can accurately infer microsatellite instability in colorectal and gastric cancers directly from standard tissue sections. Because microsatellite instability predicts robust responsiveness to immune checkpoint inhibitors, AI-assisted screening provides an immediate, cost-effective method to identify immunotherapy candidates without waiting weeks for ancillary molecular testing workflows.

Computational algorithms have demonstrated comparable capabilities in identifying diverse actionable driver mutations across other major cancer types. In non-small cell lung cancer, neural networks have accurately predicted epidermal growth factor receptor mutations from routine histology, accelerating clinical decision-making for targeted tyrosine kinase inhibitor therapies. In colorectal cancer, algorithms successfully identified KRAS and BRAF mutational signatures, which critically govern tumour aggressiveness and determine biological resistance to anti-EGFR antibody regimens. Similarly, in breast and gastric malignancies, deep learning platforms can evaluate human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 status from morphological patterns alone, offering an effective triaging mechanism to prioritize ambiguous cases for confirmatory molecular analysis. Furthermore, automated quantification of programmed death-ligand 1 expression and tumour-infiltrating lymphocytes standardizes immunotherapy stratification by overcoming the staining and sampling inconsistencies that frequently complicate manual scoring.

Surgical oncology requires exceptionally precise intraoperative and postoperative assessment of surgical resection margins and regional lymph node basins. The primary objective during cancer surgery is achieving complete microscopic tumour excision while preserving surrounding functional tissue. Positive surgical margins significantly increase local recurrence rates, frequently forcing patients to endure re-excision procedures, prolonged psychological distress, and increased medical costs. Deep learning algorithms trained on whole-slide images rapidly scan extensive tissue perimeters, identifying invasive carcinoma and ductal carcinoma in situ at margins in breast, head and neck, and gastrointestinal operations. In regional lymph node evaluation, where pathologists face visual fatigue when reviewing hundreds of microscopic fields, algorithms successfully detect minute micrometastases and isolated tumour cells.
